In [[mathematics]], a '''universal quadratic form''' is a [[quadratic form]] over a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] that represents every element of the ring.<ref name=Lam10>Lam (2005) p.10</ref>  A non-singular form over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] which represents zero non-trivially is universal.<ref name=R146>Rajwade (1993) p.146</ref>

==Examples==
* Over the [[real number]]s, the form <math>x^2</math> in one variable is not universal, as it cannot represent negative numbers: the two-variable form <math>x^2-y^2</math> over <math>\R</math> is universal.
* [[Lagrange's four-square theorem]] states that every positive [[integer]] is the sum of four [[square number|squares]].  Hence the form <math>x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + t^2 - u^2</math> over <math>\Z</math> is universal.
* Over a [[finite field]], any non-singular quadratic form of dimension 2 or more is universal.<ref name=Lam36>Lam (2005) p.36</ref>

==Forms over the rational numbers==
The [[Hasse–Minkowski theorem]] implies that a form is universal over <math>\Q</math> if and only if it is universal over [[p-adic number|{{math|'''Q'''<sub>''p''</sub>}}]] for all [[primes]] <math>p</math> (where we include <math>p=\infty</math>, letting <math>\Q_\infty</math> denote <math>\R</math>).<ref name=S43>Serre (1973) p.43</ref>  A form over <math>\R</math> is universal if and only if it is not [[Definite quadratic form|definite]]; a form over <math>\Q_p</math> is universal if it has dimension at least 4.<ref name=S37>Serre (1973) p.37</ref>  One can conclude that all indefinite forms of dimension at least 4 over <math>\Q</math> are universal.<ref name=S43/>

==See also==
* The [[15 and 290 theorems]] give conditions for a quadratic form to represent all positive integers.
